criteria.descriptor: Full marks: signature check is over the raw body with constant-time compare; HTTP status semantics are correct (2xx stops retries, 5xx only for genuinely un-accepted events); dedupe uses the event id via an atomic/unique mechanism; out-of-order handling uses event version/timestamp or state reconciliation rather than arrival order. Deduct for technically wrong claims such as verifying re-serialized JSON, returning 2xx on real failures, or calling at-least-once 'exactly-once' without a dedupe mechanism.

Full marks: addresses all four required concerns -- signature verification, fast-ACK + async processing, duplicate delivery (idempotency), and out-of-order arrival -- plus failure routing (DLQ). Partial credit scales with how many of these are covered; omitting either dedupe or ordering caps this criterion.

Full marks: justifies each mechanism with the underlying reason -- why the raw body (re-serialization breaks the HMAC), why fast ACK (the ~10s timeout triggers duplicate retries), why dedupe (at-least-once guarantees redelivery), why not trust order (backoff reorders events). Lower marks for listing mechanisms without explaining why they follow from the stated provider behaviors.

Full marks: a clear, ordered walkthrough of the handler using precise vocabulary (HMAC, idempotency key, at-least-once/effectively-once, dead-letter queue) that a reviewer could follow directly. Lower marks for disorganized or vague description that blurs the synchronous handler and the async worker.

expected_answer_points: Verify the HMAC signature over the raw, unparsed request bytes using a constant-time comparison, and reject unverified requests -- otherwise events can be forged.
Acknowledge fast: do minimal synchronous work (durably persist or enqueue the raw event) and return 2xx well within the ~10s window, processing the real work asynchronously in a worker.
Use correct HTTP semantics as the retry contract: return non-2xx (5xx) only when the event was not durably accepted so the provider retries, and never 2xx an event you dropped.
Deduplicate using the event's unique id as an idempotency key (unique constraint / atomic insert / upsert) so at-least-once delivery becomes effectively-once.
Do not rely on arrival order; order by the event's own timestamp/version/sequence (or refetch provider state) and make transitions monotonic so out-of-order retries still converge to correct state.
Make downstream side effects idempotent (e.g. pass an idempotency key), because the dedupe check and the side effect are not a single atomic action.
Handle persistent processing failures with a dead-letter queue rather than dropping events or retrying forever.
common_pitfalls: Verifies the signature over parsed-then-re-serialized JSON (or over a framework-decoded model) instead of the raw received bytes, so legitimate signatures fail -- or skips verification entirely.
Does all processing (DB writes, downstream calls, email) synchronously before responding, so slow work blows the ~10s budget and triggers a storm of duplicate retries.
Treats at-least-once delivery as exactly-once with no dedupe, so a charge or refund side effect executes twice when the event is redelivered.

Gets the retry contract backwards: returns 2xx (or a 4xx) on a genuine processing failure so the provider stops retrying and the event is lost, or returns 5xx after already committing side effects so the retry double-processes.
Assumes events arrive in the order they occurred and applies them blindly, letting a late-arriving stale event overwrite newer state (e.g. a delayed `succeeded` undoing a `refunded`).
Relies only on a check-then-insert dedupe with no unique constraint, leaving a race window where two concurrent redeliveries both pass the check and both process the event.
reference_answer:
Treat the endpoint as an ingestion point, not the place to do the real work.

1) Verify authenticity first. Compute the HMAC over the exact raw request bytes (capture the body before JSON parsing, because re-serialization changes whitespace and key order and would break the signature) using the shared secret, and compare with a constant-time function to avoid timing side-channels. On mismatch return 400/401 and stop -- this is the only thing preventing anyone from forging a `payment.succeeded`.

2) Acknowledge fast, process asynchronously. The provider retries if it doesn't see a 2xx within ~10s, so do the minimum synchronously: durably persist the raw event (or enqueue it to a queue/outbox) keyed by the provider's event id, then return 2xx. Heavy work (updating balances, emailing receipts) runs in a background worker. Return 5xx only when you could not durably accept the event, so the provider's retry is warranted; never return 2xx for an event you actually dropped.

3) Deduplicate. At-least-once means the same event id reappears. Enforce a unique constraint on event id (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT / upsert into a `processed_events` table); if it already exists, ack and skip. That turns at-least-once into effectively-once. Since the dedupe check and the side effect aren't one atomic step, also make downstream effects idempotent by passing an idempotency key to the ledger/payment system.

4) Don't trust arrival order. Backoff and retries mean a `refunded` can land before the `succeeded` it followed. Order by the event's own timestamp/version rather than receipt time, make state transitions monotonic (ignore an event that would move state backwards), or reconcile by fetching the object's current state from the provider. The goal is convergence regardless of order.

5) Handle failure explicitly. Retry transient worker failures with backoff; route repeatedly-failing 'poison' events to a dead-letter queue for inspection instead of dropping them or looping forever.
